Your digestive system can't absorb all the energy from food you eat. Try as they might, your intestines can only do so much. In fact, feces are relatively rich in nutrients; this is why you'll see some animals, for instance dogs, eat feces. This is a sign of malnourishment. Humans have a built in response to feces as disgust; even babies "know" not to eat it.

That being said, there isn't a threshold in which your body says "okay, pack it up, we're good." As long as there is food in the GI tract, specialized cells will go to work.

Stretch receptors in the stomach (which, as you probably guessed, detect the stomach lining stretch) send signals that tell chief cells (also in the stomach) to start breaking down proteins and polypeptides. Later on, they diffuse into the blood via the large intestine. There, you have special structures called "villi" that function to absorb lipids and carbohydrates. Basically, as long as there's something for those cells to do, they'll do it.

On a final note, there are some cases of food consumption in such excess that the food can't be chemically digested fast enough, and it rots in the stomach. The stomach is sort of like a bag of soup that takes chewed up food, adds some chemicals to break molecules into smaller pieces, and churns to keep everything mixed up. The pyloric sphincter, which squirts some of this soup into the small intestine, can only work so fast. If there's too much food to be processed, it sits and rots, at which point your stomach stops sending it to the intestines.

That was probably more than you wanted to know, but I'm studying this stuff and figured you might be interested!
